claim: A single exposure to brief cold-water swim stress induces prolonged activation of kappa opioid receptors (κORs) at GABAergic synapses on rat VTA dopamine neurons.
source: at GABAergic synapses on rat VTA dopamine neurons, a single exposure to a brief cold-water swim stress induces prolonged activation of κORs
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript including electrophysiology experiments showing persistent loss of LTPGABA after stress.

claim: Stress-induced κOR activation is mediated by activation of the receptor during the stressor followed by persistent, ligand-independent constitutive activation of the κOR.
source: This is mediated by activation of the receptor during the stressor followed by a persistent, ligand-independent constitutive activation of the κOR itself
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments showing that norBNI (inverse agonist) but not 6β-naltrexol (neutral antagonist) rescues LTPGABA after stress, and that 6β-naltrexol prevents loss of LTPGABA only when given pre-stress.

claim: Constitutive activity of κORs is not seen at κORs at neighboring excitatory synapses in the VTA.
source: This lasting change in function is not seen at κORs at neighboring excitatory synapses, suggesting distinct time courses and mechanisms of regulation of different subsets of κORs
evidence: Figure 5 shows that norBNI does not potentiate excitatory synapses on either Ih+ or Ih- VTA neurons in slices from stressed animals, unlike its effect at inhibitory synapses.

claim: Constitutive activity of κORs governs the prolonged reinstatement to cocaine-seeking observed after cold water swim stress.
source: We also provide evidence that constitutive activity of κORs governs the prolonged reinstatement to cocaine-seeking observed after cold water swim stress
evidence: Figure 6 shows that norBNI administered 24 hr post-stress prevents reinstatement, while 6β-naltrexol does not, indicating constitutive activity rather than ligand binding is responsible.

claim: Bath application of norBNI (100 nM) rescues LTPGABA in slices prepared 24 hr after stress in a JNK-dependent manner.
source: Representative single experiment showing that bath application of norBNI (100 nM) rescues LTPGABA in a slice prepared 24 hr after stress... norBNI does not rescue LTPGABA in the presence of the JNK inhibitor SP600125 (20 µM)
evidence: Figure 1E-H shows experimental data demonstrating that norBNI rescues LTPGABA (139 ± 7% of baseline, n=6) but not in the presence of JNK inhibitor SP600125 (106 ± 9% of baseline, n=11, p=0.029).

claim: Acute stress blocks LTPGABA, reducing IPSC amplitudes to 94 ± 11% of baseline values compared to 140 ± 5% in control animals.
source: IPSC amplitudes, control: 140 ± 5% of baseline values, n = 13; stress: 94 ± 11% of baseline values, n = 6; unpaired t-test, *p=0.0005
evidence: Figure 1B shows quantified data comparing LTPGABA magnitude between control and stressed animals with statistical analysis.

claim: The neutral antagonist 6β-naltrexol (10 µM) fails to rescue LTPGABA in slices from stressed animals.
source: Representative experiment from a cell 24 hr after stress showing that 6β-naltrexol (10 µM) fails to rescue LTPGABA... IPSC amplitudes, norBNI: 141 ± 20% of baseline values, n = 10; 6β-naltrexol: 100 ± 8% of baseline values, n = 10; unpaired t-test, *p=0.048
evidence: Figure 2D-F shows experimental data demonstrating that 6β-naltrexol does not rescue LTPGABA after stress, unlike norBNI.

claim: 6β-naltrexol (10 µM) is sufficient to block κOR-mediated depression of EPSCs by U50488.
source: Summary data showing that U50488 depresses EPSC amplitudes from VTA dopamine neurons and that 6β-naltrexol (10 µM) prevents this depression. Normalized EPSC amplitude 5–10 min after U50488: U50488 alone = 75 ± 2% of baseline values, n = 3; U50488 + 6β-naltrexol = 95 ± 1% of baseline values, n = 4; unpaired t-test *p=0.0003
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B shows that 6β-naltrexol effectively blocks U50488-induced depression of EPSCs, demonstrating the antagonist is functional at the concentration used.

claim: Pre-stress administration of 6β-naltrexol (10 mg/kg) prevents the loss of LTPGABA, but post-stress administration does not.
source: Representative experiment showing that a cell from an animal treated with 6β-naltrexol (10 mg/kg) 30 min pre-stress exhibits LTPGABA... Representative experiment showing that a cell from an animal treated with 6β-naltrexol 24 hr post-stress does not exhibit LTPGABA
evidence: Figure 3C-F shows that 6β-naltrexol pre-stress results in LTPGABA (136 ± 12% of baseline, n=12, p<0.05 from vehicle), while post-stress treatment does not (100 ± 9% of baseline, n=11).

claim: A single systemic administration of the κOR agonist U50488 (5 mg/kg) blocks LTPGABA for at least five days.
source: Representative single experiment showing a cell prepared 24 hr after a single treatment with U50488 (5 mg/kg) does not exhibit LTPGABA... Representative experiment showing that a cell prepared five days after a single treatment with U50488 does not exhibit LTPGABA
evidence: Figure 4C-F shows that U50488 blocks LTPGABA at both 1 day (108 ± 6% of baseline, n=9) and 5 days (100 ± 5% of baseline, n=10) after administration, compared to saline control (137 ± 6% of baseline, n=11).

claim: norBNI does not potentiate excitatory synapses on Ih+ VTA neurons in slices from stressed animals.
source: Representative experiment showing that norBNI does not potentiate excitatory synapses on Ih+ VTA neurons in a slice prepared from a stressed animal... No significant difference in IPSC amplitude 10–15 min after norBNI application (t-test p=0.81 IPSC amplitudes, control: 94 ± 2% of baseline values, n = 5; stressed: 92 ± 6% of baseline values, n = 6)
evidence: Figure 5B-C shows that norBNI does not affect excitatory transmission on Ih+ neurons from stressed animals, indicating constitutive activity is specific to inhibitory synapses.

claim: norBNI does not potentiate excitatory synapses on Ih− VTA neurons in slices from stressed animals.
source: Representative single experiment showing that norBNI does not potentiate excitatory synapses on Ih− VTA neurons in a slice prepared from a stressed animals... No significant difference in IPSC amplitude 10–15 min after norBNI application (t-test p=0.49 IPSC amplitudes, control: 112 ± 2% of baseline values, n = 5; stressed: 110 ± 4% of baseline values, n = 5)
evidence: Figure 5E-F shows that norBNI does not affect excitatory transmission on Ih− neurons from stressed animals.

claim: norBNI administered 24 hr post-stress prevents stress-induced reinstatement of cocaine-seeking measured 48 hr after stress.
source: norBNI (green): last extinction session: 4.8 ± 1.4 lever presses; reinstatement session: 5.2 ± 1.1 lever presses; n = 6, p=0.76, paired t-test
evidence: Figure 6B shows that animals treated with norBNI 24 hr after stress do not show significant reinstatement, unlike saline-treated controls.

claim: 6β-naltrexol administered 2 days post-stress does not prevent stress-induced reinstatement of cocaine-seeking.
source: 6β-naltrexol (blue): last extinction session: 5.7 ± 1.8 lever presses; reinstatement session: 11.2 ± 3.4 lever presses; n = 11, *p=0.033, paired t-test
evidence: Figure 6B shows that animals treated with 6β-naltrexol still show significant reinstatement, indicating constitutive activity rather than ligand binding mediates prolonged drug-seeking.

claim: Saline-treated animals show significant stress-induced reinstatement of cocaine-seeking 48 hr after stress.
source: Saline (black): last extinction session: 6.4 ± 1.7 lever presses; reinstatement session: 13.8 ± 2.4 lever presses; n = 8, *p=0.011, paired t-test
evidence: Figure 6B shows quantified behavioral data demonstrating significant reinstatement in control animals.

claim: LTPGABA is induced via activation of nitric oxide synthase in the dopamine neuron, leading to nitric oxide (NO) release, and enhancement of GABA release through cGMP signaling.
source: LTPGABA is induced via activation of nitric oxide synthase in the dopamine neuron, leading to nitric oxide (NO) release, and enhancement of GABA release through cGMP signaling
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Nugent et al., 2007, 2009) establishing the mechanism of LTPGABA induction.

claim: Acute stress blocks LTPGABA through activation of κORs.
source: we showed that acute stress blocks LTPGABA through activation of κORs
evidence: This claim references previous work (Graziane et al., 2013) and is supported by current experimental data showing rescue by κOR antagonists.

claim: Preventing κOR activation via intra-VTA administration of nor-binaltorphimine (norBNI) prevents stress-induced reinstatement of cocaine-seeking.
source: preventing this activation via intra-VTA administration of the κOR antagonist, nor-binaltorphimine (norBNI), prevents stress-induced reinstatement of cocaine-seeking
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Graziane et al., 2013) establishing the role of VTA κORs in stress-induced reinstatement.

claim: A single exposure to stress leads to a loss of LTPGABA that lasts for at least five days.
source: a single exposure to stress leads to a loss of LTPGABA that lasts for at least five days and is mediated by persistent activation of VTA κORs
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Polter et al., 2014) and is consistent with current findings.

claim: Treatment with the κOR antagonist after stress can rescue stress-induced reinstatement.
source: We have also shown that treatment with the κOR antagonist after stress can rescue stress-induced reinstatement
evidence: This claim references previous findings and is supported by current behavioral data in Figure 6.

claim: κORs decrease the firing rate of dopamine neurons through activation of GIRK channels.
source: κORs decrease the firing rate of dopamine neurons through activation of GIRK channels
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Margolis et al., 2003, 2006) establishing this mechanism.

claim: κORs inhibit excitatory synaptic transmission onto both dopaminergic and non-dopaminergic VTA neurons.
source: κORs inhibit excitatory synaptic transmission onto both dopaminergic and non-dopaminergic VTA neurons
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Margolis et al., 2005) establishing this effect.

claim: κORs reduce inhibitory synaptic transmission in a subset of dopamine neurons.
source: reduce inhibitory synaptic transmission in a subset of dopamine neurons
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Ford et al., 2006) establishing this effect.

claim: κORs inhibit somatodendritic dopaminergic IPSCs.
source: inhibit somatodendritic dopaminergic IPSCs
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Ford et al., 2007) establishing this effect.

claim: Acute and repeated stressors can escalate intake of addictive substances in animal models.
source: Animal models have shown that acute and repeated stressors can escalate intake of addictive substances
evidence: This claim cites multiple previous studies (Piazza et al., 1990; Ramsey and Van Ree, 1993; Goeders and Guerin, 1994; Shaham and Stewart, 1994; Haney et al., 1995) establishing this phenomenon.

claim: Acute stress can reinstate drug seeking in animals that have undergone extinction training.
source: acute stress can reinstate drug seeking in animals that have undergone extinction training
evidence: This claim cites multiple previous studies (Shaham et al., 1994, 1995; Conrad et al., 2010; Mantsch et al., 2016) establishing this phenomenon.

claim: Both acute stress and exposure to drugs of abuse induce a concomitant potentiation of excitatory synapses and loss of long term potentiation of inhibitory synapses in the VTA.
source: Both acute stress and exposure to drugs of abuse induce a concomitant potentiation of excitatory synapses and loss of long term potentiation of inhibitory synapses
evidence: This claim cites multiple previous studies (Ungless et al., 2001; Saal et al., 2003; Kauer and Malenka, 2007; Nugent et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2008; Niehaus et al., 2010; Polter and Kauer, 2014) establishing these synaptic changes.

claim: The JNK inhibitor SP600125 does not affect LTPGABA expression in slices from naïve animals.
source: Summary data showing that LTPGABA is expressed in slices from naïve animals in the presence of the JNK inhibitor SP600125 (20 µM). Average magnitude of LTPGABA10–15 min after SNAP = 144 ± 13% of baseline values, n = 5; one-sample t-test, p=0.0257
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1A shows that JNK inhibition alone does not prevent LTPGABA in control conditions.

claim: The JNK inhibitor SP600125 does not rescue LTPGABA in slices from stressed animals in the absence of norBNI.
source: Summary data showing that LTPGABA remains blocked in slices from stressed animals in the presence of the JNK inhibitor SP600125 (20 µM). Average magnitude of LTPGABA10–15 min after SNAP = 111 ± 11% of baseline values, n = 6; one-sample t-test, p=0.38
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B shows that JNK inhibition alone does not restore LTPGABA after stress.

claim: 6β-naltrexol does not affect basal inhibitory transmission in cells from control or stressed rats.
source: Summary data showing that 6β-naltrexol (10 µM) does not affect basal inhibitory transmission in cells from control or stressed rats. Normalized IPSC amplitude 5–10 min after 6β-naltrexol: control = 97 ± 6% of baseline values, n = 6 (4 animals); stress = 92 ± 17% of baseline values, n = 4 (2 animals); unpaired t-test p=0.79
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A shows that 6β-naltrexol does not alter baseline IPSC amplitudes.

claim: norBNI acts as an inverse agonist at κORs through JNK-dependent mechanisms.
source: Schematic of norBNI's competitive and non-competitive inhibition of κOR signaling... the requirement of JNK for norBNI to rescue LTPGABA is evidence that norBNI acts through non-competitive means
evidence: The requirement of JNK for norBNI's rescue effect (Figure 1) combined with the failure of neutral antagonist 6β-naltrexol (Figure 2) implies inverse agonist activity.

claim: Constitutive activation of κORs represents a shift in receptor conformation that is independent of ligand binding.
source: This suggests that non-competitive actions of norBNI, rather than its block of dynorphin binding, are relevant to the loss of LTP... the persistent activation of the κOR following stress does not require continuous receptor binding by ligand
evidence: The differential effects of norBNI (inverse agonist) versus 6β-naltrexol (neutral antagonist) imply a conformational change in the receptor that maintains activity without ligand.

claim: Dynorphin release during or immediately following stress triggers the shift to constitutively active κORs.
source: dynorphin release during or immediately following stress may be needed to trigger a change in the receptor leading to prolonged constitutive activation... preventing binding of dynorphin to the κOR during stress should prevent the loss of LTPGABA
evidence: The ability of pre-stress but not post-stress 6β-naltrexol to prevent loss of LTPGABA (Figure 3) implies that initial dynorphin binding is required to trigger constitutive activation.

claim: The blockade of LTPGABA by κORs likely occurs in the presynaptic terminal between activation of guanylate cyclase and enhancement of GABAergic release.
source: Because an exogenous source of nitric oxide (SNAP) does not rescue potentiation following stress, the blockade is likely to occur in the presynaptic terminal between activation of guanylate cyclase and enhancement of GABAergic release
evidence: The failure of SNAP (NO donor) to rescue LTPGABA after stress implies the block occurs downstream of NO signaling.

claim: Constitutively active κORs act on a substrate that limits induction of plasticity without affecting basal GABA release mechanisms.
source: We therefore favor a mechanism by which after acute stress, constitutively-active κORs similarly act on a substrate that limits induction of plasticity without affecting basal release mechanisms
evidence: Previous work showing no change in mIPSC frequency after stress (Graziane et al., 2013) combined with the specific loss of LTPGABA implies selective effects on plasticity mechanisms.

claim: Loss of LTPGABA results in an imbalance between inhibitory and excitatory input onto dopamine neurons.
source: LTPGABA may play a homeostatic role to enhance inhibition of dopamine neurons after strong NMDAR-activating excitation. Loss of LTPGABA, therefore, would result in an imbalance between inhibitory and excitatory input onto the dopamine neuron
evidence: The homeostatic function of LTPGABA is inferred from its mechanism of induction and the consequences of its loss.

claim: Loss of LTPGABA is likely to prolong or enhance dopamine neuron firing in response to salient stimuli.
source: As GABAergic synapses on dopamine neurons strongly control their spontaneous firing, the loss of LTPGABA is likely to prolong or enhance firing in response to salient stimuli
evidence: This inference is based on the known role of GABAergic control of dopamine neuron firing (van Zessen et al., 2012) and the loss of inhibitory plasticity.

claim: Stress produces two phases of κOR activation: an initial phase with dynorphin-mediated depression of excitatory transmission and hyperpolarization, followed by a prolonged phase with constitutive κOR activity blocking LTPGABA.
source: We might therefore predict two phases of stress-induced κOR activation. We hypothesize that dynorphin is released during and/or immediately after stress, depressing EPSCs onto dopaminergic neurons and hyperpolarizing dopaminergic neurons... However, as dynorphin is degraded, we would expect that the strength of excitatory synapses would return to normal levels while LTPGABA would become blocked by constitutive activity of κORs
evidence: This model is inferred from the differential time courses of κOR effects at excitatory versus inhibitory synapses and the mechanism of constitutive activation.

claim: The prolonged phase of constitutive κOR activity increases dopamine neuron excitability and could contribute to increased drive towards drug-seeking behavior.
source: This would instead increase the firing rate of dopaminergic neurons, particularly in response to excitatory stimuli. This increased excitability could contribute to the increased drive towards drug-seeking behavior upon exposure to spatial cues associated with past drug experience
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the inferred effects of lost inhibitory plasticity on dopamine neuron function and behavior.

claim: The firing rate of dopaminergic neurons remains elevated for several days after cold water stress.
source: Indeed, in rats subjected to the same cold water stress used in this study, the firing rate of dopaminergic neurons remains elevated for several days afterwards
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Marinelli, 2007) showing prolonged changes in dopamine neuron firing after stress.

claim: A single dose of the κOR agonist salvinorin A has biphasic effects on reward function, with immediate anhedonia followed by increased reward sensitivity at 24 hr.
source: a single dose of the κOR agonist, salvinorin A, has biphasic effects on reward function: immediately after administration, rats exhibit an anhedonic increase in reward thresholds to intracranial self-stimulation. However, 24 hr after salvinorin A administration, rats exhibit decreased reward thresholds, indicating an increase in reward sensitivity
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Potter et al., 2011) and is used to support the biphasic model of κOR effects.

claim: Dopamine neurons recorded in this study may largely comprise dopamine neurons that project to the nucleus accumbens.
source: the electrophysiological markers used here and the lateral location of our recordings within the VTA suggest to us that our population of cells may largely comprise dopamine neurons that project to the nucleus accumbens
evidence: This inference is based on the recording location and electrophysiological properties (Ih+) of the recorded neurons.

claim: Activation of VTA dopamine neurons that project to the nucleus accumbens is rewarding in mice.
source: activation of these neurons has been shown to be rewarding in mice
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Lammel et al., 2012) establishing the rewarding properties of this circuit.

claim: LTPGABA is not observed at GABAB synapses on dopamine neurons.
source: our earlier work found no LTPGABA at GABAB synapses on dopamine neurons
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Nugent et al., 2009) showing the specificity of LTPGABA to GABAA synapses.

claim: The effects of persistently activated κORs are unlikely to involve nucleus accumbens-VTA GABAergic afferents.
source: suggesting that the effects of persistently activated κORs are unlikely to involve the nucleus accumbens-VTA GABAergic afferents
evidence: This inference is based on the lack of LTPGABA at GABAB synapses, which are thought to be targeted by NAc-VTA projections.

claim: norBNI does not prevent stress from potentiating excitatory synapses on dopamine neurons.
source: the κOR block by norBNI does not prevent stress from potentiating excitatory synapses on dopamine neurons
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Graziane et al., 2013) showing the specificity of κOR effects to inhibitory plasticity.

claim: The loss of LTP at GABAergic synapses in the VTA is highly correlated with stress-induced drug-seeking.
source: Our current work confirms that the loss of LTP at GABAergic synapses in the VTA is highly correlated with stress-induced drug-seeking
evidence: This claim is supported by the parallel effects of norBNI on both LTPGABA rescue and prevention of reinstatement.

claim: κORs have shown promise as a potential drug target for substance use and mood disorders in preclinical models.
source: κORs have shown promise as a potential drug target for substance use and mood disorders... In preclinical models, κOR antagonists have shown potential efficacy for depression and for compulsive and stress-induced drug use
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Bruchas et al., 2010; Wee and Koob, 2010) establishing the therapeutic potential of κOR antagonists.

claim: Numerous clinical trials are in progress using κOR ligands to target substance use disorders and depression.
source: Numerous clinical trials are in progress using κOR ligands to target substance use disorders and depression
evidence: This claim cites multiple sources (Ehrich et al., 2015; Karp et al., 2014; Chavkin and Koob, 2016; Ling et al., 2016; Nasser et al., 2016) documenting ongoing clinical trials.

claim: Many clinical trials use buprenorphine or novel compounds which may lack inverse agonist activity at κORs.
source: However, many of these trials use buprenorphine, a partial agonist at κORs, or novel compounds which may lack inverse agonist activity, neither of which would reduce activity of constitutive κORs
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Karp et al., 2014; Rorick-Kehn et al., 2014) and raises concerns about current therapeutic approaches.

claim: Constitutive activity of κORs at inhibitory synapses in the VTA lasts only five to ten days following acute stress.
source: constitutive activity of κORs at inhibitory synapses in the VTA lasts only five to ten days following acute stress
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Polter et al., 2014) establishing the time course of constitutive activity.

claim: The duration of constitutive κOR activity (5-10 days) is considerably shorter than the typical turnover time of κORs (14-21 days).
source: a considerably shorter time period than the 14–21 days typical for turnover of κORs
evidence: This claim cites previous work (McLaughlin et al., 2004) on κOR turnover rates.

claim: Constitutive activity of κORs may be terminated by an unidentified active mechanism rather than receptor turnover.
source: This suggests that constitutive activity of the κORs may be terminated by an unidentified active mechanism
evidence: This inference is based on the mismatch between the duration of constitutive activity and receptor turnover time.

claim: GPCRs can adopt agonist-independent conformations that are constitutively active.
source: It is widely accepted that GPCRs can adopt agonist-independent conformations that are constitutively active
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Seifert and Wenzel-Seifert, 2002; Sadée et al., 2005; Young et al., 2013; Meye et al., 2014) establishing this general principle.

claim: µOR and δOR have both been shown to exhibit constitutive activity.
source: the other members of the opioid receptor subfamily, µOR and δOR, have both been shown to exhibit constitutive activity
evidence: This claim cites multiple previous studies (Wang et al., 1994, 2004; Chiu et al., 1996; Wang et al., 1999; Liu and Prather, 2001; Wang et al., 2007; Corder et al., 2013) establishing constitutive activity of other opioid receptors.

claim: κORs exhibit constitutive activity in heterologous expression systems.
source: κORs themselves have been shown to exhibit constitutive activity, both in heterologous expression systems
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Becker et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2007) demonstrating constitutive κOR activity in cell culture.

claim: κORs exhibit constitutive activity in the rat prefrontal cortex.
source: κORs themselves have been shown to exhibit constitutive activity... in the rat PFC
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Sirohi and Walker, 2015) demonstrating constitutive κOR activity in brain tissue.

claim: Signaling through the JNK pathway is responsible for the long-lasting non-competitive inhibition of the κOR.
source: Signaling through the JNK pathway is thought to be responsible for the long-lasting non-competitive inhibition of the κOR
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Bruchas et al., 2007; Melief et al., 2010, 2011) establishing the role of JNK in norBNI's effects.

claim: Inhibition of LTPGABA by κORs is likely mediated through p38 or ERK MAPK pathways, or through activation of Gαi, rather than through JNK.
source: inhibition of LTPGABA by κORs is not mediated by the JNK pathway, but instead most likely through one of the other pathways downstream of κORs, such as the p38 or ERK MAPK pathways, or through activation of Gαi
evidence: This inference is based on the failure of JNK inhibition alone to affect LTPGABA, combined with knowledge of κOR signaling pathways (Bruchas and Chavkin, 2010; Iñiguez et al., 2010; Ehrich et al., 2015).

claim: Previous exposure to a κOR agonist significantly increases constitutive activity of the receptor in heterologous cell culture systems.
source: In a heterologous cell-culture system, previous exposure to a κOR agonist alone significantly increased constitutive activity of the receptor
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Wang et al., 2007) showing agonist-induced constitutive activity in cell culture.

claim: Exposure to the µOR agonist morphine triggers an increase in constitutive activity of µORs in cultured cells and intact animals.
source: In either cultured cells heterologously expressing µORs or in intact animals, exposure to the µOR agonist morphine triggers an increase in constitutive activity of µORs
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Wang et al., 1994, 2000; Liu and Prather, 2001; Wang et al., 2004; Shoblock and Maidment, 2006; Meye et al., 2012) establishing morphine-induced constitutive µOR activity.

claim: Morphine-induced constitutive activity of µORs is regulated by calmodulin and protein kinases.
source: Morphine-induced constitutive activity of µORs is regulated by calmodulin and protein kinases
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Wang et al., 1999, 2000) establishing the molecular mechanisms of µOR constitutive activity.

claim: Under basal conditions, calmodulin binding to µORs prevents constitutive association with G-proteins.
source: Under basal conditions, calmodulin binding to the µORs prevents constitutive association with G-proteins
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Wang et al., 1999, 2000) on the mechanism of calmodulin regulation of µORs.

claim: Following morphine exposure, calmodulin dissociates from the µOR, allowing constitutive activation.
source: Following morphine exposure, calmodulin dissociates from the µOR, allowing constitutive activation
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Wang et al., 1999, 2000) on morphine-induced changes in µOR regulation.

claim: An intricate scaffolding complex regulates κOR signaling.
source: an intricate scaffolding complex regulates κOR signaling
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Bruchas and Chavkin, 2010) on κOR signaling complexes.

claim: Inflammatory pain increases constitutively active µORs in the mouse spinal cord, leading to hyperalgesia and cellular dependence.
source: it was recently reported that inflammatory pain increases constitutively active µORs in the mouse spinal cord, leading to hyperalgesia and cellular dependence
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Corder et al., 2013) showing experience-induced constitutive activity of µORs.

claim: Activation of glucocorticoid receptors is required for the block of LTPGABA by stress.
source: Our prior work indicates that activation of glucocorticoid receptors is required for the block of LTPGABA by stress
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Niehaus et al., 2010; Polter et al., 2014) establishing the role of glucocorticoid receptors.

claim: Persistent activation of glucocorticoid receptors is not seen after stress.
source: Although persistent activation of these receptors is not seen after stress
evidence: This claim references previous findings about the time course of glucocorticoid receptor activation.

claim: Coincident activation of glucocorticoid and kappa opioid receptors may lead to constitutive activation of κORs.
source: it is possible that coincident activation of glucocorticoid and kappa opioid receptors leads to constitutive activation of the latter
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms of constitutive activation based on known requirements for both receptor types.

claim: The orexin-1 receptor attenuates κOR inhibition of cAMP production but enhances recruitment of β-arrestin and p38 MAPK activation.
source: it has been reported that the orexin-1 receptor attenuates κOR inhibition of cAMP production, but enhances recruitment of β-arrestin and p38 MAPK activation
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Robinson and McDonald, 2015) on orexin-κOR interactions.

claim: Both orexin-1 receptor effects on κOR signaling are prevented by the JNK inhibitor SP600125.
source: both effects are prevented by the JNK inhibitor SP600125 used in our study
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Robinson and McDonald, 2015) on the role of JNK in orexin-κOR interactions.

claim: Both orexin and dynorphin are co-released from hypothalamic projections to the VTA.
source: Both orexin and dynorphin are co-released from hypothalamic projections to the VTA
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Chou et al., 2001; Muschamp et al., 2014; Baimel et al., 2015) on co-release of these peptides.

claim: Release of both orexin and dynorphin together, or dynorphin with another neurotransmitter, may initiate signaling events that induce synapse- or experience-selective constitutive κOR activity.
source: The putative dual receptor signaling might be one way to induce synapse- or experience- selective constitutive κOR activity
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms for selective induction of constitutive activity based on co-release patterns.

claim: LTPGABA is triggered by nitric oxide-mediated activation of cGMP-protein kinase G (PKG) signaling.
source: Our previous studies have shown that LTPGABA is triggered by nitric oxide-mediated activation of cGMP-protein kinase G (PKG) signaling
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Nugent et al., 2007, 2009; Niehaus et al., 2010) establishing the signaling mechanism of LTPGABA.

claim: The blockade of LTPGABA by stress likely occurs between activation of guanylate cyclase and enhancement of GABAergic release because SNAP does not rescue potentiation.
source: Because an exogenous source of nitric oxide (SNAP) does not rescue potentiation following stress, the blockade is likely to occur in the presynaptic terminal between activation of guanylate cyclase and enhancement of GABAergic release
evidence: This inference is based on the failure of SNAP to bypass the stress-induced block, indicating the site of action is downstream of NO.

claim: LTPGABA is lost 24 hr after a single morphine exposure.
source: LTPGABA is also lost 24 hr after a single morphine exposure
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Nugent et al., 2007; Niehaus et al., 2010) showing morphine's effects on LTPGABA.

claim: After morphine exposure, a cGMP analog or strong activation of sGC can potentiate GABA release.
source: in this situation a cGMP analog or strong activation of sGC potentiates GABA release
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Nugent et al., 2007; Niehaus et al., 2010) showing differences between morphine and stress effects.

claim: After acute stress, constitutively-active κORs may act through downregulation of soluble guanylyl cyclase or scaffolding changes that sequester PKG from its substrates.
source: We therefore favor a mechanism by which after acute stress, constitutively-active κORs similarly act on a substrate that limits induction of plasticity without affecting basal release mechanisms, perhaps through downregulation of soluble guanylyl cyclase, or scaffolding changes that sequester PKG from its substrates
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential molecular mechanisms based on the known signaling pathway and effects of κOR activation.

claim: LTPGABA is a heterosynaptic form of plasticity that can be triggered by high-frequency tetanus activating NMDAR-dependent calcium-sensitive nitric oxide synthase.
source: LTPGABA is a heterosynaptic form of plasticity that can be triggered by a high-frequency tetanus that activates NMDAR-dependent activation of calcium-sensitive nitric oxide synthase
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Nugent et al., 2007) on the induction mechanism of LTPGABA.

claim: LTPGABA would be induced when there is robust activation of excitatory inputs onto dopamine neurons.
source: We therefore expect that LTPGABA would be induced when there is robust activation of excitatory inputs onto dopamine neurons
evidence: This inference is based on the NMDAR-dependent mechanism of LTPGABA induction.

claim: LTPGABA may play a homeostatic role to enhance inhibition of dopamine neurons after strong NMDAR-activating excitation.
source: LTPGABA may play a homeostatic role to enhance inhibition of dopamine neurons after strong NMDAR-activating excitation
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the functional role of LTPGABA based on its induction mechanism and effects.

claim: GABAergic synapses on dopamine neurons strongly control their spontaneous firing.
source: As GABAergic synapses on dopamine neurons strongly control their spontaneous firing
evidence: This claim cites previous work (van Zessen et al., 2012) on GABAergic control of dopamine neuron activity.

claim: The critical role of the VTA in reinstatement of drug seeking has been repeatedly demonstrated.
source: The critical role of the VTA in reinstatement of drug seeking has been repeatedly underscored
evidence: This claim cites previous work (McFarland et al., 2004; Briand et al., 2010; Graziane et al., 2013; Mantsch et al., 2016) establishing the VTA's role in reinstatement.

claim: GABAergic synapses on VTA dopamine neurons powerfully regulate dopamine cell firing.
source: within the VTA, GABAergic synapses on VTA dopamine neurons powerfully regulate DA cell firing
evidence: This claim cites previous work (Tan et al., 2012; van Zessen et al., 2012; Polter and Kauer, 2014) on GABAergic regulation of dopamine neurons.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons were identified by the presence of a large Ih (>50 pA) during a voltage step from −50 mV to −100 mV.
source: Dopaminergic neurons, which comprise about 70% of all VTA neurons, were identified by the presence of a large Ih (>50 pA) during a voltage step from −50 mV to −100 mV
evidence: This is a methodological description of how dopamine neurons were identified in the experiments.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons comprise about 70% of all VTA neurons.
source: Dopaminergic neurons, which comprise about 70% of all VTA neurons
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about VTA cell composition.

claim: Rats were placed for 5 min in cold water (4–6°C) for the forced swim stress procedure.
source: Rats were placed for 5 min in cold water (4–6°C), then dried and allowed to recover in a warmed cage for two hours before returning to the home cage
evidence: This is a methodological description of the stress procedure used in the experiments.

claim: U50488 was administered at 5 mg/kg dissolved in saline.
source: U50488 (5 mg/kg) and 6β-naltrexol (10 mg/kg) were dissolved in saline or 10% DMSO in saline, respectively
evidence: This is a methodological description of drug preparation and dosing.

claim: 6β-naltrexol was administered at 10 mg/kg dissolved in 10% DMSO in saline.
source: U50488 (5 mg/kg) and 6β-naltrexol (10 mg/kg) were dissolved in saline or 10% DMSO in saline, respectively
evidence: This is a methodological description of drug preparation and dosing.

claim: Horizontal midbrain slices were prepared at 250 µm thickness.
source: Horizontal midbrain slices (250 µm) were prepared as previously described from deeply anesthetized Sprague-Dawley rats
evidence: This is a methodological description of slice preparation.

claim: SNAP was applied at 400 µM to induce LTPGABA.
source: induction of LTPGABA by application of the NO donor, SNAP (S-nitroso-N-acetylpenicillamine, 400 µM)
evidence: This is a methodological description of the LTPGABA induction protocol.

claim: IBMX (100 µM) was used to inhibit phosphodiesterase-mediated degradation of cGMP.
source: 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (IBMX; 100 µM) was used to inhibit phosphodiesterase-mediated degradation of cGMP and applied via perfused ACSF for at least 10 min prior to induction of LTPGABA
evidence: This is a methodological description explaining the use of IBMX in the experiments.

claim: norBNI was applied at 100 nM concentration in slice experiments.
source: NorBNI (100 nM), 6β-naltrexol (10 µM), and SP600135 (20 µM) were bath applied to slices at least 10 min prior to induction of LTPGABA
evidence: This is a methodological description of drug concentrations used.

claim: 6β-naltrexol was applied at 10 µM concentration in slice experiments.
source: NorBNI (100 nM), 6β-naltrexol (10 µM), and SP600135 (20 µM) were bath applied to slices at least 10 min prior to induction of LTPGABA
evidence: This is a methodological description of drug concentrations used.

claim: SP600125 was applied at 20 µM concentration in slice experiments.
source: NorBNI (100 nM), 6β-naltrexol (10 µM), and SP600135 (20 µM) were bath applied to slices at least 10 min prior to induction of LTPGABA
evidence: This is a methodological description of drug concentrations used.

claim: Rats were implanted with intravenous jugular catheters for self-administration experiments.
source: Rats were anesthetized with ketamine HCl (87 mg/kg, i.m.) and xylazine (13 mg/kg, i.m.) and implanted with intravenous jugular catheters
evidence: This is a methodological description of the surgical procedure for self-administration studies.

claim: Cocaine was delivered at 0.20 mg per infusion during self-administration training.
source: a response to the active lever yielded a 0.05 ml infusion of 0.20 mg of cocaine (dissolved in 0.9% saline)
evidence: This is a methodological description of cocaine dosing in behavioral experiments.

claim: Male and female Sprague-Dawley rats (P16-25) were used for slice electrophysiology studies.
source: For slice electrophysiology studies, male and female Sprague-Dawley rats (P16-25) were maintained on a 12 hr light ⁄ dark cycle and provided food and water ad libitum
evidence: This is a methodological description of the animals used in electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Male Sprague-Dawley rats (350–450g) were used for self-administration studies.
source: For self-administration studies, male Sprague-Dawley rats (350–450g) were bred in-house and individually housed in a temperature-controlled room with a 12 hr reverse light/dark cycle
evidence: This is a methodological description of the animals used in behavioral experiments.
